opening_date_evidence.text: **Economic:** The economic landscape is marked by contradictory currents of **growth and precarity**. On one hand, post-pandemic recovery and industrial policy have driven low unemployment and manufacturing investment (e.g. semiconductor fabs, clean energy projects). On the other, inflation and high interest rates have exposed systemic fragilities. The U.S. experienced in 2023 its most significant banking turmoil since 2008, as several mid-sized banks (Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank, First Republic) abruptly collapsed[en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank#:~:text=On%20March%2010%2C%202023%2C%20Silicon,and%20Signature%20Bank%2C%20in%20March). A rapid loss of confidence sparked bank runs, requiring emergency interventions to **stave off broader financial contagion**. This event highlighted how **seemingly stable systems can buckle under fast-changing conditions** (in this case, rising interest rates and tech-sector volatility), and how tightly coupled the financial “attention” is – panic can spread rapidly via digital networks. Meanwhile, at the household level, inequality and cost-of-living pressures remain extreme. Wealth concentration is high, and many Americans juggle multiple gig jobs in an increasingly **precarious labor market**. Importantly, workers have responded with a surge of collective action: 2023 saw the most major strikes in over two decades, as unions from auto workers to Hollywood writers organized work stoppages seeking fair wages and conditions[reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-labor-strikes-jump-23-year-high-2023-2024-02-21/#:~:text=Organized%20labor%20scored%20some%20major,week%20targeted%20strike). This signals that **latent energy in economic relations is being released** through labor activism – a frictional dynamic that could solidify into lasting changes in wage structures or labor laws. In summary, capital flows and labor patterns are erratic, with **old systems (e.g. low-wage gig economy, lightly regulated finance) showing strain** and new patterns (reshoring industry, union revival) emerging.

**Resistance as a signal:** Importantly, the **resistance and friction themselves are signals** of where the system is failing and where change might force its way in. The brittleness of institutions under pressure is prompting counter-movements and attempts at reform. For instance, the wave of state-level voter initiatives (from protecting abortion rights to expanding Medicaid in conservative states) represents citizens **routing around legislative gridlock** – using direct democracy as a pressure-release valve. When Florida, Kansas, and Michigan voters took matters into their own hands on contentious issues, it showed a pathway for energy to find an outlet despite institutional blocks. Similarly, grassroots resistance has grown in local governance: communities are pushing back on book bans, or forming watchdog groups to hold officials accountable, thereby **reinforcing some local democratic norms** even as national ones wobble. Labor strikes, as noted, were a key form of resistance in 2023 – they indicate that when exploitation or inequality hits a breaking point, people do activate traditional pressure tactics (picket lines, work stoppages) to force negotiation[reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-labor-strikes-jump-23-year-high-2023-2024-02-21/#:~:text=Organized%20labor%20scored%20some%20major,week%20targeted%20strike). These actions introduce friction into the economic machine in the short term (e.g. halting auto production), but they can yield rebalancing (the UAW won *“record contracts”* after their strike[reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-labor-strikes-jump-23-year-high-2023-2024-02-21/#:~:text=The%20number%20of%20strikes%20averaged,over%20the%20past%2020%20years), addressing long-festering wage disparities). In a sense, **friction can be creative**: it generates heat and light that signal where a system must adapt. Each protest, strike, or courtroom challenge is a site of potential recalibration. Of course, resistance can also harden counter-resistance – e.g. state crackdowns on protest or union busting efforts – potentially making the system even more brittle if dialogue fails. The U.S. right now is like a structure under stress tests; cracks are exposed. The hope is that recognizing these cracks (lack of trust, representational imbalances, policy paralysis) can lead to redesign or reinforcement *before* catastrophic failure.

*Workers and supporters on the UAW picket line in Michigan during the historic 2023 auto workers strike. Labor activism surged as a response to economic inequities, indicating both accumulated worker frustration and the potential for renegotiating power relationships. Such strikes are frictional events that can harden into new standards (e.g., higher wages, new work rules) if resolved successfully.*[reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-labor-strikes-jump-23-year-high-2023-2024-02-21/#:~:text=Organized%20labor%20scored%20some%20major,week%20targeted%20strike)[reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-labor-strikes-jump-23-year-high-2023-2024-02-21/#:~:text=A%20total%20458%2C900%20workers%20participated,workers%20walked%20off%20the%20job)
